title: Tesla Discloses Over $500 Million In Musk-Linked Company Revenue
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) disclosed that it generated more than half a billion dollars in revenue last year from product sales to two other Elon Musk-linked companies, adding a fresh investor focus to the commercial ties across the billionaire's business empire. In an amended annual filing uploaded Thursday, the company said about $430.1 million of that revenue came from xAI, Musk's artificial intelligence startup, while another $143.3 million came from SpaceX, his closely held rocket manufacturer. Tesla had already disclosed the xAI sales in January, but the SpaceX revenue figure was added in the amended filing, making the update potentially important for investors assessing how related-party activity may be shaping Tesla's reported revenue base.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The SpaceX disclosure comes after Bloomberg News reported earlier this month that the rocket company likely purchased more than $100 million worth of Cybertrucks in the fourth quarter of last year, a transaction that may have supported reported demand for Tesla's slow-selling electric pickup. Musk's companies have long been linked through financial investments, business agreements, and shared personnel, but the latest filing gives investors a more detailed look at how those ties are flowing through Tesla's sales. xAI buys Megapack energy storage batteries from Tesla, while Tesla has integrated xAI's Grok chatbot into its vehicles, creating a relationship that now reaches across energy storage, artificial intelligence, and the in-car software experience.

The broader setup may become even more closely watched as Musk continues to pull his companies into overlapping projects. Musk recently unveiled plans for Tesla and SpaceX to collaborate on a chip production project, while SpaceX acquired xAI in February, bringing rockets, satellites, artificial intelligence, and plans for space-based data centers under one roof. SpaceX is now attempting to stage the biggest initial public offering of all time in late June, which could place additional investor attention on how Musk's companies interact financially and strategically. Tesla also disclosed in its latest filing that it recognized about $78.1 million in revenue from xAI through February, suggesting the relationship remained active early this year and could remain a key item for investors watching Tesla's related-party revenue.

title: Solar Rout Deepens As Market Faces Possible 30% Drop
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

The US residential solar industry is facing a sharper downturn than investors may have expected after President Donald Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill ended a lucrative homeowner tax break for buying panels. Freedom Forever, one of the nation's largest solar installers, filed for bankruptcy last month, citing the phaseout of federal tax credits and Trump's executive orders aimed at limiting the growth of renewables. The pressure is spreading across the biggest national names in home energy, with Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), Enphase Energy (NASDAQ:ENPH), SolarEdge Technologies (NASDAQ:SEDG) and Sunrun (NASDAQ:RUN) all reporting soft first-quarter sales. This has added to analyst concerns that the rooftop solar market could shrink as much as 30% this year. Joe Osha, a clean energy analyst at Guggenheim Securities who recently dropped coverage of Sunrun, described the industry as a zero-growth sector, underscoring how quickly sentiment has shifted from expansion to retrenchment.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The weakness has been building for several years. Higher interest rates have made it more expensive for homeowners to finance solar systems that can cost $20,000 or more, while tariffs on solar imports from Southeast Asia have raised equipment costs and squeezed margins. California, the largest home solar market, also reduced state incentives for new solar-only systems starting in 2023, putting more pressure on demand. Against this backdrop, Sunrun's major national rivals SunPower and Sunnova Energy International filed for bankruptcy in 2024 and 2025, respectively. The Trump administration's law may now be the industry's biggest hurdle, ending the homeowner solar tax credit at the end of last year, rapidly phasing out a federal subsidy available to companies that lease residential solar systems, and introducing new anti-China restrictions that have made some longtime bank participants hesitant. Enphase Chief Executive Officer Badri Kothandaraman said the market is going through a major disruption and that residential solar is being rebuilt right now.

For investors, the near-term picture remains difficult, even as rising utility bills should theoretically make rooftop solar more attractive. Ohm Analytics expects second-quarter solar interconnections to decline by more than a quarter from the same period a year earlier, and the firm forecasts a 22% decline for the full year. Enphase shares have fallen nearly 30% from their year-to-date high in early February, while Sunrun dropped close to 40% after reporting fourth-quarter earnings in late February before rebounding as much as 23% on Thursday after first-quarter earnings and sales topped analyst estimates. SolarEdge has moved in the opposite direction, rising about 40% so far this year partly on hopes for stronger sales in Europe, where power prices have jumped from the war in Iran. Battery storage could be one possible path through the downturn, helped by falling costs and tax-credit eligibility through 2033. In California, about 90% of solar panels sold now come with a battery, according to Ohm Analytics, while states including Texas, California and New York are establishing or developing policies that reward homeowners for participating in distributed power plant programs. Sunrun, which says it has built the nation's biggest home battery network, sees the current market dislocation as a possible chance to gain share, while SolarEdge Chief Executive Officer Shuki Nir said there could be short-term hiccups but long-term demand remains present.

title: Tesla Stock Shrugs Off Massive Vehicle Recall
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) is recalling more than 218,000 vehicles over a rear view camera issue, but investors are barely reacting as the fix is largely software based and already rolled out to most affected cars.

The recall impacts several models, including the Model 3, Model Y, Model S and Model X, with some vehicles dating back to 2017. The issue involves delayed rear camera images, which could increase crash risk if drivers do not see approaching vehicles in time. Tesla said the problem only affects vehicles running HW3 hardware and noted there have been no reported crashes, injuries or fatalities tied to the issue so far.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

What kept the market calm is how the company handled it. Tesla said affected vehicles simply need updated firmware, and more than 99.9% of impacted cars have already downloaded the fix remotely. That continues to highlight one of Tesla's advantages compared to traditional automakers, where recalls often require physical dealership visits and higher repair costs.

Separately, Tesla also filed new trademark applications tied to the long delayed Roadster, fueling speculation that the vehicle could finally move closer to launch. The filings reportedly came with intent to use status, suggesting Tesla may be preparing for eventual commercial rollout.

title: China's Robot Lead Could Lift Manufacturing Share To 16.5%
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Morgan Stanley economists have projected that China's early lead in humanoid robots could help drive the next phase of the country's global manufacturing and export strength. In a report led by chief Asia economist Chetan Ahya, the bank said China's share of global manufacturing could rise to 16.5% by 2030, up from 15% today, as the country builds out capacity across the humanoid robotics supply chain. The setup echoes China's earlier push into electric vehicles and batteries, where early planning and large-scale investment helped create a dominant industrial position. Ahya noted that China has a record of identifying major growth areas early and preparing ahead of time, adding that robotics appears to be following a similar path. Over the past couple of years, humanoid robotics has begun moving from the lab into the real world, with Chinese tech parks, factories and universities already deploying humanoids, while government procurement is also starting to support broader adoption.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The race is no longer just a technology story. It is becoming another front in the wider strategic competition between China and the US, with American firms such as Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) also investing heavily in humanoid robots. Morgan Stanley said the US has generally focused on high-cost, high-spec prototypes and testing before scaling production, while Chinese firms have moved faster to roll out models and use the domestic market as a proving ground. That speed could possibly give China an edge, especially because competitors including the US, Japan and South Korea often rely on Chinese inputs and components. The momentum has already caught investor attention, with Chinese media regularly reporting new progress in humanoid robotics. A red humanoid recently completed a half-marathon in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, about seven minutes faster than the men's world record, and robotics shares jumped after the news.

Still, Morgan Stanley's message is not just about upside. The humanoid robot market is attracting billions of dollars of investment, but the technology remains far from proven in terms of real-world value. Protectionism could become a risk, much as Chinese EVs have faced tariffs and restrictions in global markets. Although humanoid robotics is still a new industry, which means there may be fewer existing producers and workers to protect, concerns over security and technical dependence could still rise. The other pressure point is supply. Morgan Stanley warned that excessive investment and intense competition could create a production glut, pushing automation-equipment prices lower. That could be a double-edged sword for investors: cheaper robots could possibly accelerate global adoption, support productivity and help contain end-product inflation, but too much supply expansion may also hurt pricing power and industry returns.

title: Musk's Tesla-SpaceX Chip Plan Could Reach $119 Billion
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Elon Musk's semiconductor plan is becoming one of the biggest capital allocation stories around Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX, and the numbers are hard for investors to ignore. A public notice says SpaceX estimates that a next-generation, vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing fabrication facility planned with Tesla would cost at least $55 billion, with total capital investment possibly rising to $119 billion if additional phases are completed. The project may be located in Grimes County, Texas, near the Gibbons Creek Reservoir and surrounding areas, though Musk said on X that the site is only one of several locations under consideration. The hearing notice, scheduled for June 3, described the facility as a potentially transformative investment in domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity, putting the Terafab plan directly at the center of Musk's broader push into AI, robotics and space.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The scale of the proposal matters because SpaceX is looking to raise around $75 billion from a record IPO that would value the company at more than $2 trillion, according to Bloomberg reporting cited in the source text. That means the chip facility's larger buildout could possibly exceed the amount SpaceX aims to raise from the offering. Musk first detailed the SpaceX-Tesla Terafab project in March, saying the companies needed to build their own chip capacity because the semiconductor industry was moving too slowly to support his robotics, space and artificial intelligence projects, as well as wider tech demand. His framing was blunt: We either build the Terafab or we don't have the chips, and we need the chips, so we build the Terafab. The facility would aim to produce 2 nanometer chips and could one day support a terawatt of computing power per year, the amount Musk expects the companies to eventually use as AI and robotics spending ramps higher.

For investors, the opportunity comes with a heavy execution burden. The source text notes immediate skepticism after Musk outlined the plan, because advanced chip manufacturing is complex, competitive and dominated by companies such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (NYSE:TSM), while Musk has no track record in running advanced fabs. Still, Musk's team has already moved to gather supplier intelligence, with lieutenants reaching out to Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT), Tokyo Electron Ltd. and Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) for equipment price quotes and delivery times. Musk also struck a partnership with Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), under which Tesla plans to spend roughly $3 billion on a research chip facility in Texas while Intel contributes chip design, fabrication and packaging expertise. The spending question is becoming harder to separate from the investment case: Tesla said in April that capital expenditures in 2026 will exceed $25 billion, up from a prior forecast of around $20 billion and roughly three times last year's outlay, while Tesla shares have fallen more than 20% from a mid-December record high. SpaceX is also ramping spending, after saying in April it had struck an agreement for the right to acquire artificial intelligence startup Cursor for $60 billion later this year, or pay $10 billion for the companies' work together. The Terafab plan could be a defining test of whether Musk's AI, robotics and space ambitions can justify an increasingly aggressive capital spending curve.

title: OpenAI Tesla Merger Idea Emerges In Trial
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) CEO Elon Musk once pushed to bring OpenAI into Tesla and even offered OpenAI CEO Sam Altman a seat on Tesla's board, according to testimony from former OpenAI board member Shivon Zilis.

The comments came during an ongoing court battle tied to Musk's lawsuit against OpenAI, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT).

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Zilis testified that between 2017 and 2018, OpenAI's leadership debated different corporate structures extensively, including whether the AI company should evolve into a for-profit business. At one point, Musk reportedly proposed folding OpenAI into Tesla as part of that process.

The testimony adds another layer to the increasingly public split between Musk and OpenAI. Musk co-founded the company in 2015 and reportedly contributed about $38 million in early funding before leaving the board in 2018 after disagreements over control. He is now suing OpenAI and its leadership for more than $130B, arguing the organization abandoned its nonprofit mission. OpenAI has pushed back, saying Musk understood the company's commercial ambitions from early on.

The trial also highlights how closely tied the early AI ecosystem was to major tech and automotive players before the current AI boom reshaped the industry. Since leaving OpenAI, Musk launched xAI, which has since merged with SpaceX, creating a direct competitor in the AI race.
